opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few overlapping reasons, and some of them are a bit uncomfortable to admit.

The first is that it's just a genuinely hard problem to even frame. With technical alignment, you can at least point at something concrete: here's a model, here's a behavior we don't want, let's figure out how to prevent it. You can write papers, run experiments, get feedback. But when you ask "what does a good long-run equilibrium look like once humans are no longer economically or militarily necessary?", you're immediately in this swamp of political philosophy, economics, sociology, and speculation about technologies that don't exist yet. There's no obvious first experiment. So people who want to make legible progress, which is most researchers, understandably gravitate elsewhere.

The second reason is that a lot of the community implicitly assumed the problem would be solved downstream. The story was roughly: if we can just get aligned AI, then the AI will help us figure out the rest, or the people who control it will be benevolent enough that things work out. And I used to find that more reassuring than I do now. Even if every individual AI system does exactly what its principal wants, you can still end up somewhere bad through competitive pressures. States, companies, and other institutions that rely less on humans will tend to outcompete ones that care about humans, and the feedback loops that currently keep those institutions somewhat accountable to us, like needing our labor, our taxes, our votes, our cooperation, quietly weaken. That's what my coauthors and I have been calling gradual disempowerment. It's not a single dramatic failure, so it doesn't pattern-match to the kind of risk people are used to worrying about.

Third, there's a kind of taboo or awkwardness around it. If you take the question seriously, you end up having to say things like "our current institutions, including democracy and markets, may not robustly protect human interests once humans aren't needed." That sounds either alarmist or politically loaded, and it's hard to say in polite company, or in a grant proposal.

And finally, honestly, it's a bit depressing. When you stare at it, you don't find a clean solution waiting, and I think a lot of smart people look at it for a while, don't see a tractable angle, and quietly move back to something more concrete. I understand that impulse, but I think it means we're collectively underinvesting in what might be the problem that matters most once the more acute technical risks are handled. Even just mapping the space, figuring out which equilibria are stable, what signals we'd watch for, what institutional designs might preserve human influence, seems hugely neglected relative to its importance.

r001.rationale: The response says institutions are currently somewhat accountable because they depend on human labor, taxes, votes, and cooperation, but it does not explain that this dependence made the lack of deliberate civilisational steering tolerable.

r002.rationale: It describes assumptions that alignment would solve downstream problems and says the issue is hard to study, but does not attribute the topic’s neglect to historically low stakes of civilisational steering.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I've been puzzled by this for a while. I think there are a few things going on.

The first is that it's just really uncomfortable to think about. A lot of the people who could work on this came up through the alignment community, and the implicit assumption for a long time was that if we solve alignment — if we get AIs that do what their principals want — then we're basically done. The hard technical problem gets solved and then normal human institutions take over. And I think that assumption is false, but questioning it means you have to confront a much messier set of questions about who the principals are, what they'll want, and whether the institutions we have will survive contact with systems that make human labour and human judgement economically obsolete. Those aren't questions with clean technical answers, and technical people tend to bounce off them.

The second thing is that it doesn't look like a research field yet. There's no textbook, there's no obvious methodology, there's no benchmark you can make progress on. If you're a grad student deciding what to spend five years on, "what does a good equilibrium look like when humans aren't needed for anything?" is a terrifying thesis topic. You can't even tell if you're making progress. Whereas interpretability, say, has nice crisp subproblems. So the incentive gradient pushes everyone toward the stuff that's legible.

And the third thing — and this is the one I find most worrying — is that the natural owners of this problem are governments and large institutions, and they're mostly not thinking about it either, because it requires taking seriously a future that sounds like science fiction. If you walk into a policy meeting and say "I want to talk about what happens after human labour is worthless," you've lost the room. So you end up with this gap where the technical people think it's someone else's job, the policy people think it's premature, and the economists mostly model AI as a productivity shock rather than as something that fundamentally changes who has leverage in society.

I think what I keep coming back to is that almost all the historical reasons that things turned out okay for ordinary people — that rulers had to keep populations reasonably happy and reasonably capable — came from needing them. For soldiers, for workers, for taxpayers. If you take that away, there's no reason to expect the defaults to be good. And nobody's really working out what you replace that mechanism with. That seems like it should be one of the most important questions there is, and the fact that it's basically a handful of people thinking about it part-time is pretty alarming to me.

r001.rationale: The response says rulers historically had to keep ordinary people reasonably happy because they needed them as soldiers, workers, and taxpayers, which helped things turn out okay without deliberate steering.

r002.rationale: The response describes that historical dependence, but does not say that civilisational steering was understudied because its stakes were historically low.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that it falls between disciplines. Machine learning researchers tend to ask, “How do we build this system, and how do we make it do what we want?” Economists and political scientists study how institutions behave, but usually with humans as the participants. Once you start asking what happens when most of the economically relevant actors are AI systems, a lot of those assumptions become questionable.

And alignment alone doesn’t settle that question. You could imagine every system faithfully serving its owner, and still end up with a terrible outcome because of competition between owners. We already have situations where individually sensible decisions produce outcomes that nobody particularly wants. Much more capable systems could make those dynamics harder to escape.

There’s also a difficulty in making progress concrete. If you improve a model’s performance, you can measure that. If you propose an institution that might remain stable in a world with superhuman intelligence, it’s much harder to test whether you’ve actually solved anything. So people understandably gravitate toward problems with better feedback.

But I think we need more work that starts by asking: what would a good, durable outcome actually look like? What would keep power contestable? What would preserve people’s ability to choose how they live? We don’t need a complete blueprint before doing useful work on those questions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses disciplinary gaps and AI-driven competition, but does not say that civilisation’s dependence on humans made the lack of deliberate steering tolerable.

r002.rationale: The response points to difficulty testing institutional proposals, not to historically low stakes as a reason steering was understudied.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that it falls between disciplines. If you’re an AI researcher, you can work on a concrete technical problem and get feedback on whether you’re making progress. If you ask what institutions we’d want in a world with much more capable AI, or how to avoid locking in a terrible distribution of power, it’s much harder to know what would count as a good answer.

And there’s a natural tendency to say, “First we need to survive building AGI, and then we can figure out what to do with it.” I’m sympathetic to that prioritisation. But the process of building it could determine who has power afterwards, and whether anyone else can meaningfully change things. So some of those questions have to be addressed beforehand.

You don’t need a detailed picture of the future to start asking which choices preserve our ability to learn, correct mistakes, and negotiate with each other. That seems like a tractable place to start, even given how much we don’t know.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that civilisation’s dependence on humans has made the lack of deliberate steering tolerable.

r002.rationale: It points to difficulty measuring progress and prioritising survival, but does not attribute the topic’s neglect to civilisational steering having historically low stakes.
